definition: The Cranfield experiments were a series of experimental studies in information retrieval conducted by Cyril W.
details: Cleverdon in the 1960s at the College of Aeronautics, today known as Cranfield University, to evaluate the efficiency of indexing systems. The experiments were broken into two main phases, neither of which was computerized. The entire collection of abstracts, resulting indexes and results were later distributed in electronic format and were widely used for decades. In the first series of experiments, several existing indexing methods were compared to test their efficiency. The queries were generated by the authors of the papers in the collection and then translated into index lookups by experts in those systems. In this series, one method went from least efficient to most efficient after making minor changes to the arrangement of the way the data was recorded on the index cards. The conclusion appeared to be that the underlying methodology seemed less important than specific details of the implementation. This led to considerable debate on the methodology of the experiments. These criticisms also led to the second series of experiments, now known as Cranfield 2. Cranfield 2 attempted to gain additional insight by reversing the methodology; Cranfield 1 tested the ability for experts

explainer.lead: The Cranfield experiments were an early effort to compare indexing systems by testing how efficiently they handled the same collection and queries. Their lasting lesson was double-edged: controlled comparisons are valuable, but small implementation choices can distort what those comparisons appear to prove.

tiers.eli5: Imagine testing several ways of labelling boxes of cards to see which helps you find answers fastest. Cyril W. Cleverdon did something similar with research abstracts and indexing systems in the 1960s. One method jumped from worst to best after small changes to its index cards, showing that the setup of a test can matter as much as the idea being tested.
tiers.practitioner: Treat Cranfield as an experimental design for controlled comparisons, not as software to install. Keep the collection and queries fixed while changing the indexing method, and inspect implementation details before attributing performance differences to the underlying approach. When using the later electronic collection, remember that the original experiments themselves were not computerized.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, Cranfield 1 compared indexing systems over a shared collection of abstracts: paper authors generated queries, and experts in each system translated those queries into index lookups. Conducted by Cyril W. Cleverdon in the 1960s at the College of Aeronautics, the experiments found that minor changes to index-card data arrangement could reverse an efficiency ranking. This implementation confound prompted methodological debate and Cranfield 2, which reversed the methodology.

explainer.example: In the first series, one indexing method initially ranked least efficient. After minor changes to how its data were arranged on index cards, it became the most efficient, suggesting that implementation details could outweigh the underlying methodology.

explainer.intuition: To compare ways of organizing information fairly, give them the same material and questions. Then check whether the result reflects the indexing method itself or merely the way that method was implemented.
howItWorks: Have the papers' authors generate queries.
Let system experts translate queries into index lookups.
Compare the efficiency of the indexing methods.
Revise the methodology when implementation effects cloud the comparison.
explainer.whyItMatters: The experiments exposed how easily implementation choices can confound comparisons of indexing systems. They also produced an electronic collection of abstracts, indexes and results that supported information retrieval research for decades.
misconceptions: The original experiments were not computerized.
The results did not prove that indexing methods never differ.
Cranfield 2 was a methodological reversal, not merely a computer rerun.

diagram.caption: Cranfield 1 used shared abstracts and author-generated queries to compare indexing methods; criticism of the results led to Cranfield 2.
